newsitem.title: USA: White House treats report on FBI gingerly.
newsitem.headline: White House treats report on FBI gingerly.

text.p: The White House on Tuesday tiptoed around a published report that the FBI denied its request for information about alleged Chinese efforts to meddle in U.S. politics, saying it did not know if information was withheld.

The New York Times reported on Tuesday that the Federal Bureau of Investigation denied a White House request for "sensitive counterintelligence information" about Beijing's alleged plans to involve itself in U.S. politics.

Quoting U.S. officials, the newspaper reported that FBI Director Louis Freeh rebuffed a request last month by White House Counsel Charles Ruff for material to brief Secretary of State Madeleine Albright before a trip to China.
The White House has said Albright raised the issue of the alleged Chinese effort -- which China has strongly denied -- in her talks in Beijing last month.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry declined to confirm or deny the New York Times story, telling reporters the White House requested information and received a response. He would not say if it was satisfied by the information provided.

Asked if Clinton was troubled by the possibility the FBI may have withheld information he might need for official duties, McCurry said: "I'm not confirming or denying that that is the case. I don't know whether that is true or not.

"I think the president would be disturbed if any information necessary for the conduct of his official duties was withheld from him. I don't know whether that happened or not ... We made our request and we've gotten back what we've gotten back."

McCurry's cautious response reflected a sensitivity to White House dealings with the FBI that dates to alleged White House misuse of the federal law enforcement agency during the purge of the White House travel office in 1993.
It also reflected administration sensitivity to reports China may have sought to funnel money to the Democratic Party during last year's presidential campaign, allegations China has denied.

The White House and the FBI engaged in an unusual public spat last month over a 1996 briefing the FBI gave mid-level officials at the National Security Council about the alleged Chinese efforts. The White House said the NSC officials were told not to brief their superiors on the matter, which the FBI flatly contradicted. Eventually, the White House and FBI suggested there may have been a misunderstanding in the matter.

According to the newspaper, Ruff wrote Deputy Attorney General Jamie Gorelick on Feb. 18 asking what federal investigators knew about China's alleged involvement. An answer was prepared but Freeh, travelling in the Middle East at the time, intervened to have the document withheld, the paper said, citing federal law enforcement officials.
Ultimately, after Freeh consulted with Attorney General Janet Reno, the paper said, the Justice Department provided some information to the White House.
